The Common tody-flycatcher (Todirostrum cinereum) is a small passerine inhabiting lowland forests across much of the Neotropics. Under controlled laboratory conditions at a metabolic chamber temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], respirometry trials on post-absorptive individuals yielded a basal metabolic rate of 30.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 30.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns with the elevated metabolism characteristic of tiny Tyrannidae. This measurement was obtained from adult birds weighing approximately 6.25 grams [Wwi = approximately 6.25 grams], which represents the typical ultimate wet weight for females of this species. Adult males tend to be slightly heavier, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 7.1 grams [Wwi = 7.1 grams], a modest but consistent sexual size dimorphism observed across multiple field studies. These mass data were compiled from museum specimen series and live captures throughout their range.

Field studies of Todirostrum cinereum have documented that females lay 2 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per clutch], with approximately 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 clutch per year], yielding an annual reproductive output that reflects the consistently warm ambient conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] during the peak breeding season. The nests are typically pear-shaped structures suspended from thin branches, and each clutch contains between two and three eggs, though multiple nesting attempts can occur across the year. Reproductive activity appears tightly linked to the rainy season when insect prey becomes abundant, enabling the sustained provisioning effort required by the altricial young.

The incubation period for fertilised ova takes place at a slightly lower temperature, with eggs maintained at an average of 32 °C [T = 32 °C] by the incubating adult, and hatching occurs after an incubation duration of 18 days [ab = 18 days] at that temperature. This duration is relatively short compared to larger tyrannids, reflecting the rapid embryonic development permitted by the warmer thermal environment typical of lowland tropical nests. Newly hatched chicks exhibit an initial wet body mass of just 1.13 grams [Ww0 = 1.13 grams], a value recorded from broods in Costa Rica. This negligible mass at the moment of hatching underscores their extreme altricial state, requiring sustained brooding and frequent prey deliveries from both parents to meet the daily energetic costs of rapid tissue growth.

Developmental milestones for nestling Todirostrum cinereum are tightly scheduled under the sustained warmth of the Neotropical climate, typically around 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The age at fledging, when the pin-feathered chicks achieve their first flight, is 18 days after hatching [tx = 18 days after hatching], among the shortest nestling periods recorded for the Tyrannidae at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. On a slower developmental schedule, the onset of puberty or sexual maturation occurs at 54 days after hatching [tp = 54 days after hatching], a comparatively rapid attainment of reproductive capacity for a small tropical passerine at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The timing of these transitions is undoubtedly accelerated by the high ambient temperatures, which reduce the energetic costs of thermoregulation for the developing nestlings, allowing more resources to be directed toward feather growth and gonadal maturation.

Long-term records from banding studies in central Panama have revealed that the maximum lifespan for Todirostrum cinereum is approximately 6.5 years [am = approximately 6.5 years] when measured under natural field conditions at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. First successful breeding occurs at about 0.96 years after birth [tR = about 0.96 years after birth] under the same thermal at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]regime. This relatively early onset of reproduction, combined with a moderate reproductive output and a lifespan exceeding half a decade, defines a fast-slow axis typical of many small-bodied tropical birds that balance high adult survival against modest annual fecundity in a comparatively stable environment.
